strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem—exposure bias / the closed-loop gap in autoregressive action-conditioned robot world models—with clear practical relevance for using world models as policy-evaluation environments.

The method is clearly motivated and well-specified: the adaptation of the contrastive DiffusionNFT objective to the x0-prediction (EDM) parameterization is described precisely, the group-relative branching protocol (shared prefix, K candidates, group normalization) is a sensible solution to the lack of a fixed 'prompt' in autoregressive video, and full pseudocode and hyperparameters are provided (Alg. 1), supporting reproducibility.

The evaluation is unusually comprehensive: metrics against multiple baselines (WPE, IRASim, Ctrl-World) on the DROID validation split, object-/robot-centric masked evaluations that guard against background-preservation artifacts, a blind 2AFC human preference study with statistical analysis, temporal-degradation curves, and a world-model-to-real policy correlation experiment (Pearson r and MMRV) that speaks to the actual use case.

The ablation study (Appendix B) is extensive (learning rate, reward composition, prefix sampling vs. curriculum, group size, horizon, view weighting, KL regularization, EMA schedules), and is honest enough to report configurations where simpler or alternative choices are competitive or better.

The theoretical appendix provides a complete, self-contained derivation showing the optimal predictor moves along the reward-aligned direction, with a clean argument for why the objective is parameterization-agnostic.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental. The core training signal is a direct adaptation of DiffusionNFT [42]; the 'theory' amounts to the observation that an affine output mapping preserves the objective construction, which the authors themselves show is straightforward. Moreover, the concurrent WorldCompass [36] already applies contrastive RL post-training with prefix rollouts to a world model; the remaining deltas (randomized prefix horizon, x0 parameterization, multi-view reward design) are useful but modest, and no empirical comparison to [36] is provided.

The reward requires held-out ground-truth future frames for the executed actions. This is feasible on pre-recorded DROID trajectories but limits the framework's applicability to the very use case motivating the work (simulating novel policies in novel states), where no ground truth exists. The paper does not clearly discuss this limitation.

Several ablation results are inconsistent with the authors' design choices: best-of-2 and group size 4 outperform the chosen group-size-16/best-of-5 configuration, prefix range {0..4} slightly beats {0..9}, and policy EMA (Table 11) outperforms the no-EMA configuration. The justifications ('stability', 'efficiency') are qualitative, and many reported differences (e.g., KL regularization, EMA schedules) appear to be within noise, weakening the ablation-based support for specific choices. The main results (Table 1, 14-step rollouts) and ablation numbers (10-step rollouts) are also not directly comparable.

The human preference study is small in scale: 8 in-house raters, moderate inter-rater agreement (κ ≈ 0.4), and the binomial p-value treats votes as independent, which is questionable with only 8 raters and self-selected videos.

Gains on the wrist camera—the view the paper emphasizes as most critical—are modest in absolute terms (LPIPS 0.310→0.277, SSIM 0.62→0.67), and the policy-evaluation correlation improvement is small (r 0.796→0.822) on only 3 tasks with few rollouts, though the MMRV improvement is more convincing.
No explicit statement of code/model release, which matters for reproducibility given the dependence on a reproduced Ctrl-World baseline.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and important problem (exposure bias / error compounding in autoregressive robot world models) that is well motivated and clearly articulated.

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough: full-frame metrics, object- and robot-centric masked metrics, per-frame temporal degradation curves, a 2AFC human preference study with statistical analysis, and a downstream policy-evaluation correlation experiment (Appendix C) that goes beyond raw visual fidelity.

The derivation in Appendix A is complete and self-contained; the extension of the contrastive objective from velocity prediction to x0-prediction via the affine EDM preconditioning is correct, and the parameterization-agnostic discussion is a useful clarification.
The training protocol is described at a level of detail (pseudocode, hyperparameters, reward weights, compute budget) that supports reproducibility.
The ablation section is honest, e.g., openly reporting that best-of-2 and group size 4 outperform the configuration used for the main results.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty over prior and concurrent work. The core update rule is directly adopted from DiffusionNFT [42], and concurrent work [36] already applies contrastive RL post-training to world models with a prefix-rollout strategy. The remaining deltas — an x0-parameterization adaptation (which the authors themselves show is a straightforward affine substitution with 'no additional correction terms'), a random instead of fixed prefix schedule, and averaging LPIPS/SSIM/PSNR over three views — are incremental engineering rather than a substantive methodological advance.

The ablations undercut the paper's own design narrative. The random prefix schedule (a headline contribution) is only marginally better than the fixed schedule, the curriculum of [36], and even a shorter random range (0–4 beats 0–9 on several metrics). Best-of-2 and group size 4 outperform the chosen best-of-5 / group size 16 used for the main results. This means (a) the reported state-of-the-art numbers are not from the strongest configuration by the authors' own evidence, and (b) the central design-choice claims are weakly supported.

The reward requires held-out ground-truth future frames conditioned on the executed actions, so post-training is restricted to replaying dataset trajectories. This limits the claimed value of the world model as a closed-loop simulator for arbitrary policies: the improvement regime (on-distribution action sequences with available GT) is narrower than the deployment regime the introduction emphasizes.

The perceptual-reward objective incentivizes matching ground-truth pixels/features, which risks pushing the model toward the conditional mean of the data rather than genuinely better dynamics; the masked evaluations mitigate but do not fully rule out this concern, and no reward-hacking analysis (e.g., behavior on out-of-distribution actions) is provided.

The theoretical claims are overstated relative to their content. Theorem 1 assumes unlimited capacity, an exactly converged reference posterior mean, and a particular probabilistic reading of the reward; the resulting 'policy-improvement guarantee carries over exactly' framing in the abstract and contributions suggests more than what is actually shown.

Evaluation is confined to a single base model (Ctrl-World) and a single dataset (DROID); there is no evidence of generality of the recipe across backbones or embodiments. Some main-paper ablation metrics also use 10-step rollouts while headline results use 14-step, an inconsistency that complicates cross-checking.

The human study, while statistically significant, involved only 8 in-house raters who were allowed to select which videos to rate, introducing potential selection effects; the moderate inter-rater agreement (κ ≈ 0.4) is acknowledged but not resolved.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly written paper addressing the practically important exposure-bias/rollout-gap problem in action-conditioned video diffusion world models, with a well-structured problem formulation (Sec. 3.1) that convincingly explains why teacher-forced training cannot fix the closed-loop gap.

Solid empirical evidence: consistent improvements over Ctrl-World across all metrics on DROID (Table 1), with masked object- and robot-centric evaluations (Table 2) that show gains are task-relevant rather than background artifacts — this is a thoughtful and unusual evaluation design.

Extensive and honest ablation studies (Appendix B) covering learning rate, reward composition, prefix sampling, group size, horizon, view weighting, KL, and EMA schedules, reported at matched gradient-update counts, which is more rigorous than much of the RL-for-diffusion literature.

A complete, self-contained theoretical derivation (Appendix A) showing the contrastive objective transfers to x0-prediction EDM parameterizations, with a proof that the minimizer moves in the reward-aligned direction; the parameterization-agnostic remark at the end of App. A is a nice touch.

Evaluation goes beyond perceptual metrics: a blind 2AFC human study with ELO ranking, and a world-model-to-real correlation experiment (App. C) measuring Pearson correlation and MMRV on task progression — this directly probes the downstream use case that motivates the work.
Full pseudocode (Alg. 1) and implementation details improve reproducibility; limitations and future work are discussed concretely.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental relative to concurrent work. The core method is an adaptation of DiffusionNFT [42], and the concurrent WorldCompass [36] already applies contrastive RL post-training with a prefix rollout strategy to a world model. The stated deltas (randomized vs. fixed prefix horizon, x0-prediction adaptation, multi-view rewards) are real but modest; notably, there is no head-to-head comparison against the full [36] method — only against its curriculum schedule within the authors' own framework (Table 5). This weakens the claim of a clear advance over the closest related work.

The reward requires held-out ground-truth frames paired with the executed action sequence. This makes the method applicable only to replayed, pre-recorded trajectories and limits its utility for simulating novel policies or counterfactual actions — arguably the main use case for world-model simulators. The policy-evaluation experiment (App. C) is small (3 tasks, 3 policies, 5 real / 11 simulated rollouts per cell) and does not fully resolve this concern.

Several of the authors' own ablations undermine the final configuration choice: 'No best-of-N' beats the default 'Best-of-5' on all metrics, and 'Best-of-2' is best overall (Table 6); fixed prefix sizes 3 and 0–4 match or beat the default (Table 5); w_wrist=2 improves wrist metrics (Table 8). The post-hoc justifications (efficiency, stability) are plausible but the defaults look suboptimal by the paper's own evidence, and these inconsistencies are not fully reconciled.

The human study has notable weaknesses: only 8 in-house raters (potential affiliation/confirmation bias), moderate inter-rater agreement (κ ≈ 0.4), and raters were allowed to choose which videos to rate, introducing selection bias. The very high preference (80%) may be inflated by these design choices even if the binomial significance is strong.

Missing hyperparameter details hurt reproducibility: the mixing coefficient β and branch length F are central to the method (Eq. 1–2, Alg. 1) but their values never appear to be specified; no code release is mentioned.

The '~98% win rate' in Sec. 4 is based on paired metric differences, not human judgments — a model can improve a metric on nearly all samples while the perceptual gain is negligible on many; the framing slightly overstates this result.

The theoretical result assumes unlimited model capacity and a well-calibrated reward-as-probability model, and its practical guidance is limited; the paper does not empirically test the predicted 2/β scaling or distribution-shift effects of contrastive training on rollout diversity, which is a known failure mode of such objectives.

No comparison to simpler exposure-bias mitigations (e.g., input perturbation [26], scheduled sampling, or noise-augmented history conditioning) as baselines, making it hard to judge how much of the gain specifically requires the RL machinery versus simply training on imperfect histories.

strengths: Addresses an important, well-motivated problem (exposure bias / closed-loop error compounding in action-conditioned robot world models) that limits the practical utility of state-of-the-art world models like Ctrl-World.

Technically careful adaptation of the contrastive RL objective (DiffusionNFT) from velocity-prediction flow matching to EDM x0-prediction, with a complete, self-contained derivation and a policy-improvement theorem in Appendix A showing the guarantees carry over; the parameterization-agnostic connection is a genuine (if modest) theoretical contribution.

The branching protocol (frozen shared prefix as the group-relative context, uniformly sampled prefix depth) is a clean and sensible solution to the lack of a fixed prompt in autoregressive video, and is supported by an ablation against fixed and curriculum schedules.

Very thorough experimental validation beyond the headline metrics: SOTA on DROID vs. three baselines across all metrics, paired-difference distributions (~98% win rate), object-/robot-centric masked evaluations showing gains are not background artifacts, generalization to Bridge and RT-1, world-model-vs-real policy evaluation correlation (0.822 vs 0.796), a real-robot policy improvement experiment (+19% task progression), a blind 2AFC human study with ELO, and an unusually extensive ablation suite (learning rate, reward composition, prefix strategy, group size, best-of-N, KL, EMA variants, horizon).

The comparison against an HPSv3-based reward (Table 13) directly engages the closest concurrent work (WorldCompass) despite acknowledging that head-to-head comparison is precluded, and isolates the transferable component (reward design).
Honest limitations section, including computational overhead and the absence of physics/geometry-aware rewards.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental. The core machinery is a re-derivation of DiffusionNFT for a different parameterization plus an engineering-level branching/reward protocol; the closely related concurrent WorldCompass [41] shares the core motivation and paradigm (prefix rollouts, contrastive RL post-training), narrowing the conceptual delta to the x0 derivation, randomized prefix horizon, and lightweight rewards. This is best viewed as an Algorithms/General contribution where the empirical case, rather than conceptual novelty, must carry the paper.

The reward fundamentally requires held-out ground-truth frames aligned with the action trajectory at training time, which limits generality of the framework and makes the RL objective resemble on-policy imitation. Notably, the Self-Forcing-style baseline (training on own rollout history but regressing ground truth) achieves quite close metrics (e.g., 0.872/25.52/0.116 vs 0.868/25.35/0.119 external), suggesting a substantial fraction of the gain comes from on-policy data exposure rather than the contrastive RL objective specifically; margins on several metrics are within plausible noise and no variance/significance is reported for that comparison.

A potential inconsistency in the theory: Theorem 1 states the optimal predictor moves (2/β)Δx0 from the reference, implying the shift grows unboundedly as β→0, yet Sec. 3.2 states β→0 recovers standard supervised denoising against the reference. This tension (whether Δx0 scales with α/β in a compensating way) deserves clarification; as written, the interpretation of the theorem's β-dependence appears contradictory.

The reported main configuration is not the best-performing one by the paper's own ablations: group size 4, best-of-2, and policy EMA all outperform the defaults (Tables 6, 11), with the authors' justification (stability/efficiency) stated only qualitatively. This weakens the rigor of the 'conservative default' claim and creates a mismatch between ablation-best and reported main results (Table 13 even uses top-k=2 while the main config is best-of-5).

Reproduction discrepancy in Table 1: the reproduced Ctrl-World numbers (PSNR 23.02, LPIPS 0.081) differ noticeably from the published ones (23.56, 0.091), and the wrist-camera comparison is only against the authors' own reproduction; this raises questions about strict comparability of the headline SOTA claim.

The human study is small (8 in-house expert raters, moderate inter-rater κ≈0.4), and raters could self-select which videos to rate, which could bias the 80% preference figure; the binomial test supports the sign of the result but not the magnitude.

No analysis of potential reward hacking or diversity collapse from optimizing frame-wise perceptual metrics against ground truth (e.g., effect on stochastic scene elements), nor of compute cost of rollout generation beyond a brief remark.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and well-motivated problem (exposure bias / compounding error in autoregressive robot world models) with a coherent technical approach: adapting contrastive RL post-training (DiffusionNFT) to x0-prediction EDM parameterizations and to autoregressive video where no fixed 'prompt' exists for group-relative comparison.

The branching protocol (shared prefix, K candidate continuations, group-normalized rewards) is a sensible and clearly explained mechanism for recovering the shared-context structure required by group-relative RL in the autoregressive setting.

Experimental evidence is unusually broad for this kind of paper: rollout fidelity metrics on DROID against multiple baselines, masked object-/robot-centric evaluations, temporal degradation curves, generalization to Bridge and RT-1 embodiments, comparison to a Self-Forcing-style baseline and to the HPSv3 reward of WorldCompass, world-model-to-real policy evaluation correlation, and a small real-robot policy improvement experiment.

An extensive ablation suite (learning rate, reward combination, prefix sampling, group size/best-of-N, horizon, view weighting, KL and EMA regularization) with an honest accounting of which choices are within measurement noise, plus pseudocode and a self-contained derivation in the appendix supporting reproducibility.
Limitations are discussed meaningfully, including the computational overhead of K=16 candidates and the lack of physics/geometry-aware rewards.
weaknesses: Novelty is substantially limited by the concurrent WorldCompass work [41], which already applies contrastive RL post-training with prefix rollouts to world models; the deltas here (x0- vs v-prediction re-derivation, randomized vs fixed prefix schedule, different reward design) are incremental, and the ablations in Tables 5 and 9-11 show the randomized-prefix choice itself yields gains within noise, weakening the claimed differentiation.

The reward is computed by comparing generated frames against held-out ground-truth trajectories. This conflates 'world model fidelity' with 'reproducing the specific demonstrated trajectory' and is only well-defined on dataset distributions; it cannot reward off-distribution or open-ended rollouts, raising a concern that post-training partly encourages deterministic replay/memorization of DROID trajectories rather than genuine closed-loop dynamics modeling. The paper does not test how the model behaves under actions that deviate from demonstrated data.

The headline theoretical claim that 'convergence guarantees carry over exactly' is overstated: Theorem 1 holds under unlimited data and capacity, assumes the reference model already equals the posterior mean, and the resulting optimal predictor shifts by 2/β·∆x0 — which appears to conflict with the text's claim that larger β produces a stronger signal. The theory is a fairly direct affine reparameterization rather than a new result.

The human preference study is small (8 raters, 217 votes), conducted in-house with expert raters who may be affiliated with the authors, and inter-rater agreement is only moderate (κ ≈ 0.4); the policy improvement experiment involves a single task, 50 rollouts, and 5 trials per block, so the +19% claim has wide uncertainty.

Evaluation of rollout quality against ground-truth frames at 5 Hz for ~11 s is a relatively short horizon for claims of 'persistent' world models; evidence on much longer horizons where baselines fully decohere is not provided.

Some ablation conclusions are internally awkward: best-of-2 and EMA-on-policy configurations outperform the chosen defaults (Tables 6, 11), yet the more conservative settings are retained, so the reported main results are not the best configuration the authors themselves identify.

strengths: Addresses an important, well-motivated problem: exposure bias / error compounding in autoregressive robot world models, which directly limits their use as simulators for policy evaluation and improvement.

Solid technical contribution: adapting the DiffusionNFT contrastive objective to x0-prediction EDM backbones is non-trivial, and the self-contained derivation in Appendix A (posterior mixture decomposition, Theorem 1) is clear and verifies that policy-improvement guarantees transfer without σ-dependent corrections.

The training protocol observation — that the frozen history buffer state at a rollout step plays the role of the prompt in group-relative objectives, enabling branching of comparable candidate continuations — is a clean and sensible solution to a real structural gap between image and autoregressive video generation.

Unusually thorough evaluation for this area: quantitative rollout metrics vs. three baselines, object/robot-masked metrics showing gains are task-relevant rather than background artifacts, a 2AFC human preference study with statistical reporting, WM-to-real policy evaluation correlation (Pearson r and MMRV across three tasks and three policies), a small real-robot policy improvement experiment, and generalization to Bridge and RT-1 embodiments.

Extensive ablation studies (learning rate, reward composition, prefix sampling strategy, group size, best-of-N, horizon, view weighting, KL, EMA variants) with honest reporting, including the finding that uniform random prefix sampling outperforms the curriculum of concurrent work [41], and a direct reward-design comparison against HPSv3 that isolates the transferable component relative to WorldCompass.

Clear positioning against concurrent work [41] with specific, testable distinctions (randomized prefix vs. fixed schedule, x0 vs. v-pred, multi-view manipulation rewards, human/robot-centric validation).
weaknesses: The theoretical claims are somewhat oversold relative to their content. Theorem 1 holds only under unlimited capacity, exact posterior means, and an idealized reward-as-probability interpretation (r(x0,c)=P(o=1|x0,c)); group z-score normalization, clipping, best-of-N subsampling, and LoRA-only updates all deviate from the analyzed objective. Statements like 'convergence guarantees carry over exactly' should be softened.

Rewards are computed against held-out ground-truth frames for pre-recorded trajectories, so post-training optimizes fidelity to dataset-consistent futures rather than true closed-loop dynamics. The masked evaluations mitigate the background-preservation concern, but the paper does not fully rule out reward hacking toward metric-realisable appearance rather than physically correct dynamics; the authors' own limitations section acknowledges no physics/geometric constraints.

Several ablations show the shipped default configuration is not the best-performing one (e.g., best-of-2 beats best-of-5, prefix range 0–4 slightly beats 0–9, no policy EMA beats policy EMA, KL regularization helps five of six metrics yet the narrative around Table 9 is muddled). Using a 'conservative default' is defensible, but it makes the main-table numbers not the method's best-known configuration and raises questions about the consistency of hyperparameter selection across experiments (also 14-step main rollouts vs. 10-step ablation rollouts complicates cross-referencing).

Novelty is incremental relative to DiffusionNFT [47] and the concurrent WorldCompass [41]; the contribution is an adaptation plus protocol design. The paper handles this fairly, but the margin over a Self-Forcing-style baseline (train on corrupted history + GT regression) is modest on some metrics, so the value of the RL objective specifically rests partly on reward curves rather than end metrics.

The human study has only 8 in-house raters (likely affiliated with the authors), with moderate inter-rater agreement (κ≈0.4); despite strong statistics, an independent or larger-scale study would be more convincing.

The real-robot policy improvement experiment is small (one task family, 5 trials/block, 50 finetuning rollouts), and the reported +19% over Ctrl-World is not accompanied by variance or significance analysis.

Some notation and reporting inconsistencies (H used both for history length and prediction horizon in ablations; baseline reproduction numbers differ from published numbers in Table 1 without much discussion).
